                                   Project Number 58481


 Rulemaking to Implement Large                            Public Utility Commission of
 Load Interconnection Standards                                        Texas
      Under PURA § 37.0561


Comments from Competitive Power Ventures on Proposal for Publication
                     of New 16 TAC §25.194
Competitive Power Ventures, Inc. (“CPV”) appreciates the work of the Public Utility Commission of
Texas (“PUCT”) Commissioners and Staff on the important issue of large load interconnection and
implementation of Senate Bill 6 (2025) and PURA §37.0561. We thank you for the opportunity to
provide our input on the Proposal for Publication and believe that the state will identify the best
path forward to protect ratepayers while also supporting economic development and the continued
growth of an industry important to the U.S. economy and our national security.

CPV has included below several recommendations that we believe will enhance the proposal
broken into “critical issues” and “additional considerations.” The critical issues raised, if not
addressed appropriately, could hinder any new merchant development. Additional considerations
are offered as recommendations to improve the process:

                                          Critical Issues

      CPV recommends breaking the interconnection process into two phases to better align
       ﬁnancial commitments with project maturity and technical feasibility.

Under the current proposal, an interconnecting large load would have to pay an application fee and
put signiﬁcant ﬁnancial security at risk prior receiving sufficient information to determine whether
the project is technically feasible or economically viable. This approach will discourage speculative
projects but would likely also limit otherwise viable projects.

To address this issue, CPV recommends a two-step process prior to execution of an
interconnection agreement:

Phase 1 – Application and Feasibility Study

The ﬁrst step should require a non-refundable application fee to start an initial feasibility-level
study. This study should evaluate high-level transmission constraints, identify the potential need for
network upgrades, and provide preliminary cost and timeline estimates.

The proposed study fees of $100,000 for large loads between 75 MW and 250 MW and $300,000 for
large loads greater than 250 MW should be sufficient to cover the cost of conducting the feasibility
 study while also serving as a meaningful deterrent to speculative and non-viable projects. This
initial screening process supports the Commission’s goal of “minimizing the potential for stranded
infrastructure costs,” without imposing unnecessary ﬁnancial risk at the earliest stages of project
development.

Phase 2 – Financial Commitment and Advancement

After receiving the results of the feasibility study, large load projects that wish to proceed would be
required to post ﬁnancial security based on their requested peak demand. At this stage, project
sponsors will have greater clarity into system impacts, required upgrades, and project economics
that will enable a more informed investment decision.

Requiring ﬁnancial security after feasibility results ensures that only projects with a credible path
forward advance in the interconnection process. This strengthens queue discipline for developers
and preserves market access for economically strong projects.

This phased approach also aligns with other interconnection processes where early-stage studies
inform go/no-go decisions prior to signiﬁcant ﬁnancial security decisions.

       CPV recommends lowering the ﬁnancial security commitment from $50,000 per MW to
        between $10,000 and $15,000 per MW and increasing the 20% eligible refund to 50%.

CPV supports the establishment of ﬁnancial security requirements as a necessary tool to promote
queue discipline; however, CPV does not support the proposed requirement of $50,000 per MW.
Further, we have signiﬁcant concerns with 80% of this security being non-refundable until ﬁve years
after the site reaches full energization.

This proposed level of ﬁnancial security does not appear to align with actual interconnection or
upgrade costs and is disproportionate to the information available to a project at this stage of the
interconnection process. For example, a large load seeking 1.8 GW of power would face a
ﬁnancial security commitment of $90 million. Requiring a substantial and mostly non-refundable
ﬁnancial commitment introduces a signiﬁcant development risk without a corresponding beneﬁt to
reliability or cost causation principles.

CPV recommends that the Commission adopts a ﬁnancial security commitment in the range of
$10,000 to $15,000 per MW following a feasibility study phase. This range is more appropriate in
this phase of the project and that this level of commitment can be more clearly linked to study and
eventual upgrade costs known during this phase of the interconnection process. Aligning ﬁnancial
obligations with available information helps to ensure that ﬁnancial security serves its intended
purpose without creating undue barriers to entry.

Additionally, at such an early stage, CPV recommends increasing the eligible refund percentage
from 20 percent to 50 percent. Under the current proposal, placing 80 percent of security at risk for
an extended period – potentially for years – creates a major disincentive for an otherwise viable
project. This is exacerbated in a development process, like large load facilities, where project
timelines, customer commitments, and infrastructure evolve in parallel.
 CPV supports efforts to limit speculative projects; however, the proposed provision does not
allocate risk in a balanced manner. CPV’s recommendation will preserve ﬁnancial accountability
while recognizing the uncertainty present in early stages of large load projects.

                                      Other Considerations

      CPV recommends that the interconnection fee be applied to security requirements
       after execution of the interconnection.

At execution of the interconnection agreement, the initial interconnection fee should be credited
towards the ﬁnancial security requirements related to signiﬁcant equipment or services, and
system upgrades. The remaining ﬁnancial security should exist to cover potential differences in
interconnection costs, and additional work as needed. As the interconnection progresses, the
ﬁnancial security requirement should decline to reﬂect costs as they are recovered by the
transmission service provider or distribution service provider. This meets the intent of minimizing
the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining reliability while also reducing the
excess ﬁnancial commitment of the large load that would be tied up during the interconnection
process as project risk decreases.

      CPV recommends allowing for minor capacity request changes without requiring a new
       interconnection application and losing security.

CPV believes it is reasonable to allow for minor changes (up to 10%) in capacity request from large
loads during the interconnection study phase. We recognize that multiple changes or signiﬁcantly
larger capacity requests can disrupt the study process, but minor changes should not create such
substantial impacts to necessitate a completely new request, nor should it put ﬁnancial security at
risk. During the development process, which occurs parallel to the interconnection process, these
minor modiﬁcations are common and should be allowed.

      CPV recommends that the window for execution of the interconnection agreement be
       increased from 30 days to 60 days.

Immediately prior to the execution of the interconnection agreement, a developer will have several
ﬁnancial commitments in addition to conﬁrming project economics that may take multiple weeks
to coordinate with lenders, partners, and regulators. A 60-day window would provide much needed
additional time to ﬁnalize these commitments, especially given the signiﬁcant funds due at
execution in this proposed process.

Thank you for considering CPV’s comments and recommendations and we look forward to
continuing to work with the Commission and Staff to ensure continued economic development in
the State of Texas while also preventing harmful impacts to ratepayers.
 Respectfully submitted,



Thomas J. Rumsey
EVP, Sustainability & External Affairs



Dated: April 6, 2026
                                    Executive Summary
                                  Competitive Power Ventures



CPV recommends the following critical issue changes to ensure the Commission’s goals while also
providing optimal signals for development.

      CPV recommends breaking the interconnection process into two phases to better align
       ﬁnancial commitments with project maturity and technical feasibility.
   •   CPV recommends lowering the ﬁnancial security commitment from $50,000 per MW to
       between $10,000 and $15,000 per MW and increasing the 20% eligible refund to 50%.

Additionally, CPV requests consideration of the following recommendations to enhance the
proposed large load interconnection process.

      CPV recommends that the interconnection fee be applied to security requirements after
       execution of the interconnection.
      CPV recommends allowing for minor capacity request changes without requiring a new
       interconnection application and losing security.
      CPV recommends that the window for execution of the interconnection agreement be
       increased from 30 days to 60 days.
